title: Book I: Miss Brooke — Chapter IX
paragraphs:
1st Gentleman. An ancient country, ancient oracles
Called “thirsty for law”: its every struggle sought
Order and perfect governance.
Tell me, where are such countries now? . . .
2nd Gentleman. Where they always were—in human souls.

Mr. Brooke found Mr. Casaubon's conduct over the marriage settlements entirely satisfactory. The preparations moved smoothly forward, making the weeks of courtship seem shorter. The bride-to-be must visit her future home and specify whatever changes she wanted. A woman gives orders before marriage to develop an appetite for obedience afterwards. Certainly the mistakes we mortals, male and female, make when allowed our own way might reasonably cause surprise that we enjoy it so much.

On a grey but dry November morning, Dorothea drove to Lowick with her uncle and Celia. Mr. Casaubon lived in the manor house. Nearby, visible from parts of the garden, stood the little church, opposite the old parsonage. At the beginning of his career he had held only the parish living, but his brother's death had given him the manor too. Its small park contained fine old oaks here and there, and an avenue of lime trees approached the south-west front. A sunken fence divided park from pleasure grounds, so the drawing-room windows offered an uninterrupted view down a grassy slope, past the limes, into level cornfields and pasture that often seemed to dissolve into a lake beneath the setting sun. This was the house's happy side. The south and east looked rather mournful even on the brightest morning. There the grounds were more cramped, the flower beds poorly tended, and large clumps of trees, mostly gloomy yews, rose high less than ten yards from the windows. Built of greenish stone in the old English style, the house was not ugly, but its small windows gave it a melancholy look. It was the sort of place that needed children, abundant flowers, open windows and little glimpses of bright things to appear a joyful home. In this late autumn, with a few remaining yellow leaves drifting across dark evergreens in sunless stillness, the house itself seemed in autumnal decline. When Mr. Casaubon appeared, he had no bloom for such a background to emphasize.

“Oh dear!” Celia thought. “I'm sure Freshitt Hall would have been nicer.” She imagined its white freestone, columned porch and flower-filled terrace, with Sir James smiling above the flowers like a prince emerging from enchantment in a rosebush, his handkerchief newly transformed from its sweetest petals. Sir James, who talked so agreeably, always of sensible things and never of scholarship! Celia possessed the light, youthful feminine tastes that solemn, weather-beaten gentlemen sometimes prefer in wives. Fortunately Mr. Casaubon's preference was different, since he would have had no chance with her.

Dorothea, by contrast, found everything she could wish for in house and grounds. The dark shelves in the long library, carpets and curtains faded by time, odd old maps and bird's-eye views along the corridor walls, with an antique vase here and there beneath them—none oppressed her. They seemed more cheerful than the casts and pictures at the Grange, brought home by her uncle from his long-ago travels, probably among the ideas he had once absorbed. To poor Dorothea those austere classical nudes and simpering Renaissance-Correggio effects were painfully inexplicable, staring into the heart of her Puritan view of things. Nobody had taught her how to connect them with her own life. Lowick's owners apparently had not travelled, and Mr. Casaubon's studies of the past did not employ such aids.

Dorothea explored the house with delighted feeling. Everything seemed sacred. This would be the home of her married life. Whenever Mr. Casaubon drew attention to some particular arrangement and asked if she wanted it changed, she looked up at him with complete trust. She received each appeal to her taste gratefully, but saw nothing to alter. His painstaking courtesy and formal tenderness seemed flawless. Every blank she filled with unseen perfections, interpreting him as she interpreted Providence, blaming apparent discords on her own inability to hear the higher harmonies. Courtship leaves many such blanks for loving faith to fill with happy certainty.

“Now, my dear Dorothea, please do me the favour of choosing which room you would like for your private sitting room,” Mr. Casaubon said, showing that his conception of feminine nature was broad enough to accommodate this need.

“It's very kind of you to think of it,” Dorothea replied, “but I assure you I'd rather have all such matters decided for me. I'd be much happier with everything just as it is, the way you're used to it, or whatever arrangement you choose yourself. I have no reason to wish for anything else.”
“Oh, Dodo,” Celia said, “why not have the upstairs room with the bow window?”

Mr. Casaubon led them there. The bow window looked down the lime avenue. All the furnishings were faded blue, and a cluster of miniature portraits showed ladies and gentlemen with powdered hair. A tapestry above a door displayed another blue-green world, with a pale stag in it. The slender-legged chairs and tables looked easy to knock over. One could imagine a tightly laced lady's ghost returning to the scene of her embroidery. A light bookcase holding small calf-bound volumes of polite literature completed the room.
“Yes,” Mr. Brooke said, “this would be pretty with new curtains and sofas and that sort of thing. It's a little bare at present.”

“No, uncle,” Dorothea said eagerly. “Please don't suggest changing anything. So much else in the world needs changing; I'd like to accept these things as they are. And you like them as they are, don't you?” she added, looking at Mr. Casaubon. “Perhaps it was your mother's room when she was young.”
“It was indeed,” he replied, bending his head slowly.
“This is your mother,” Dorothea said, turning to study the miniatures. “It's like the tiny portrait you brought me, though I'd think it a better likeness. And the one opposite—who is she?”
“Her older sister. Like you and your sister, they were their parents' only children. Their parents' portraits hang above, as you see.”

“The sister is pretty,” Celia remarked, implying less approval of Mr. Casaubon's mother. It opened a new prospect to her imagination that he belonged to a family whose members had all once been young, the ladies wearing necklaces.

“It's an unusual face,” Dorothea said, examining it closely. “Those deep grey eyes set rather close together, and the delicate, irregular nose with a sort of ripple in it, and all the powdered curls falling backwards. Altogether I'd call her unusual rather than pretty. She doesn't even have a family resemblance to your mother.”
“No. Their fortunes were not alike either.”
“You haven't told me about her,” Dorothea said.
“My aunt made an unfortunate marriage. I never met her.”

Dorothea wondered a little, but felt it would be tactless just then to ask for details he did not volunteer. She turned to admire the view through the window. The sun had recently broken through the grey, and the lime avenue cast shadows.
“Could we walk in the garden now?” Dorothea asked.

“And you'll want to see the church, you know,” Mr. Brooke said. “A curious little church. And the village. It's all tucked into a nutshell. It will suit you, Dorothea, by the way. The cottages look like a row of almshouses—little gardens, gillyflowers, that kind of thing.”
“Yes, please,” Dorothea said, looking at Mr. Casaubon. “I'd like to see all of it.” His most vivid description of Lowick's cottages so far had been that they were “not bad.”

Soon they followed a gravel path running mostly between grassy edges and clumps of trees, the shortest route to the church, Mr. Casaubon said. At the small churchyard gate they stopped while he went to the nearby parsonage for a key. Celia had lagged behind, but came forward when she saw he had gone. In her easy, clipped way, which always seemed to deny any suspicion of malice, she said—
“Do you know, Dorothea, I saw someone quite young coming along one of the paths.”
“Is that so surprising, Celia?”
“There might be a young gardener, you know—why not?” Mr. Brooke suggested. “I told Casaubon he ought to change his gardener.”
“No, it wasn't a gardener,” Celia said. “A gentleman with a sketchbook. He had light brown curls. I only saw him from behind, but he was quite young.”
“The curate's son, perhaps,” Mr. Brooke said. “Ah, Casaubon's coming back with Tucker. He's going to introduce him. You haven't met Tucker yet.”

Mr. Tucker was the middle-aged curate, one of the “inferior clergy,” who generally have no shortage of sons. But after the introduction nothing in the conversation prompted a question about his family, and everyone except Celia forgot the startling appearance of youth. She privately refused to believe that those light brown curls and that slender figure could be related to Mr. Tucker, who looked exactly as old and musty as she would have expected Mr. Casaubon's curate to look. Doubtless he was an excellent man destined for heaven—Celia did not wish to lack principle—but the corners of his mouth were so unpleasant. She rather gloomily imagined her time at Lowick as bridesmaid, while the curate probably had no pretty little children she could like without reference to principle.

Mr. Tucker proved invaluable on the walk; perhaps Mr. Casaubon had foreseen this. The curate answered all Dorothea's questions about the villagers and other parishioners. Everyone in Lowick was comfortable, he assured her. Every tenant of those low-rent paired cottages kept a pig, and the strips of back garden were well maintained. The little boys wore excellent corduroy; the girls became tidy servants or did some straw plaiting at home. There were no looms, no religious Dissent. Though people generally preferred saving money to cultivating spirituality, vice was rare. Speckled hens were so numerous that Mr. Brooke observed, “I see your farmers leave some barley for the women to glean. The poor here could have a chicken in the pot, as that good French king wished for all his people. The French eat plenty of chickens—scrawny chickens, you know.”
“I think that was a very cheap wish,” Dorothea said indignantly. “Are kings such monsters that a wish like that counts as a royal virtue?”
“And if he wished them a scrawny chicken,” Celia added, “that wouldn't be nice. But perhaps he wanted them to have fat ones.”

“Yes, but that word has vanished from the text, or perhaps was subauditum—that is, present in the king's mind but unspoken,” Mr. Casaubon said, smiling and inclining his head towards Celia. She immediately fell back a little, unable to bear his blinking at her.

Dorothea became silent on the return to the house. She felt disappointed, and ashamed of the disappointment, that Lowick offered her nothing to do. For a few minutes she considered how much she would have preferred discovering that her future home lay in a parish with a greater share of the world's misery, where she could take on more active duties. Then, returning to the future actually before her, she pictured a more complete devotion to Mr. Casaubon's aims, while she waited for new responsibilities. The higher knowledge their companionship would give her might reveal many.
Mr. Tucker soon left: parish work prevented him from lunching at the Hall. As they passed through the little gate into the garden again, Mr. Casaubon said—
“You seem somewhat sad, Dorothea. I hope what you have seen has pleased you.”

“I feel something perhaps foolish and wrong,” she replied with her usual candour. “Almost wishing people here needed more help. I've known so few ways of making my life useful at all. Naturally my ideas of usefulness must be narrow. I need to learn new ways to help people.”
“Undoubtedly,” Mr. Casaubon replied. “Every position brings its appropriate duties. I trust yours as mistress of Lowick will leave none of your aspirations unsatisfied.”
“I do believe that,” Dorothea said earnestly. “Please don't think I'm unhappy.”
“That is good. But if you are not tired, let us return to the house by a different route from the one we took before.”

Dorothea was not tired at all. They took a short detour towards a fine yew, the chief inherited glory of the grounds on this side. Approaching it, they saw a figure seated on a bench sketching the old tree, conspicuous against the dark evergreens. Walking ahead with Celia, Mr. Brooke turned and asked—
“Who's that young man, Casaubon?”
They were quite close by the time Mr. Casaubon replied—
“A young relation of mine, a second cousin. In fact,” he added, looking at Dorothea, “he is the grandson of my aunt Julia, the lady whose portrait you were examining.”
The young man put down his sketchbook and stood. His abundant light brown curls and youthful appearance immediately identified him as the figure Celia had seen.
“Dorothea, may I introduce my cousin, Mr. Ladislaw? Will, this is Miss Brooke.”

He was close enough now that when he lifted his hat, Dorothea saw grey eyes set rather near together, a fine irregular nose with a little ripple, and hair falling backwards. His mouth and chin, however, were more pronounced and challenging than those in his grandmother's miniature. Young Ladislaw apparently felt no need to smile as if delighted to meet his future second cousin by marriage and her relations. He wore instead a rather sulky expression of discontent.
“You're an artist, I see,” Mr. Brooke said, picking up the sketchbook and leafing through it with his usual lack of ceremony.
“No, I only do a little sketching. There's nothing there worth seeing,” young Ladislaw said, reddening, perhaps from annoyance rather than modesty.

“Oh, come, here's a nice bit. I used to do a little of this myself, you know. Now look here: this is what I call a nice thing, done with what we used to call _brio_.” He held out to the girls a large coloured sketch of rocky ground, trees and a pool.

“I'm no judge of such things,” Dorothea said, not coldly but eagerly protesting the appeal to her opinion. “You know, uncle, I never see the beauty in those pictures you tell me everyone praises. They're a language I don't understand. I suppose there's a connection between pictures and nature that I'm too ignorant to feel, just as you can see the meaning of a Greek sentence that says nothing to me.” She looked up at Mr. Casaubon, who inclined his head, while Mr. Brooke smiled casually and said—

“Bless me, how different people are! But you were taught badly, you know. Otherwise this is just the thing for girls—sketching, fine art and so forth. Instead you took to drawing plans. You don't understand _morbidezza_ and that sort of thing. I hope you'll visit me and let me show you what I used to do in this line,” he continued, turning to Ladislaw, whose absorbed scrutiny of Dorothea had to be interrupted. Ladislaw had decided she must be an unpleasant girl, since she was marrying Casaubon. Even had he believed her professed stupidity about pictures, it would have confirmed his opinion. Instead, he heard a concealed criticism and felt sure she thought his sketch dreadful. Her apology was too clever: she was mocking both him and her uncle. But what a voice! Like the voice of a soul that had once inhabited an Aeolian harp. Nature must be inconsistent here. A girl capable of marrying Casaubon could have no passion of any kind. Still, he turned away and bowed his thanks for Mr. Brooke's invitation.

“We'll look through my Italian engravings together,” the good-natured man continued. “I've endless things like that, put away for years. One gets rusty in this part of the country, you know. Not you, Casaubon; you stick to your studies. But my best ideas get buried at the bottom, fall out of use, you know. You clever young men must watch out for laziness. I was too lazy myself; otherwise there was a time when I might have been anywhere.”
“A timely warning,” Mr. Casaubon said. “But we should go on to the house now, in case the young ladies are tired of standing.”

Once their backs were turned, Ladislaw sat down to resume his sketch. Amusement spread over his face as he worked, until finally he threw back his head and laughed aloud. Partly the reception of his artistic effort entertained him, partly the idea of his solemn cousin as that girl's lover, and partly Mr. Brooke's description of the position he might have reached but for laziness. Mr. Will Ladislaw's sense of absurdity lit his face very pleasantly. It was sheer enjoyment of the comic, without a trace of sneering or self-importance.
“What's your nephew going to do with himself, Casaubon?” Mr. Brooke asked as they continued walking.
“You mean my cousin, not my nephew.”
“Yes, yes, your cousin. But what career, you know?”

“The answer is painfully uncertain. After Rugby he refused an English university, where I would gladly have sent him, and chose what I must consider the irregular course of studying at Heidelberg. Now he wants to go abroad again without any definite aim beyond a vague intention of what he calls culture: preparation for he knows not what. He refuses to choose a profession.”
“I suppose he has no income except what you supply.”

“I have always led him and his friends to understand that I would provide, within reason, what was needed for a scholarly education and a respectable start in life. I am therefore obliged to fulfil the expectations I created,” Mr. Casaubon said, presenting his behaviour as a matter of simple duty. Dorothea admired this delicacy.
“He's eager to travel. Perhaps he'll become a Bruce or a Mungo Park,” Mr. Brooke suggested. “I once had some idea of that myself.”

“No, he has no inclination to explore or to expand our geognosis, our knowledge of the earth. That would be a definite aim I could approve to some extent, though I would not congratulate him on choosing a career so often ending in an early, violent death. Far from wishing for more precise knowledge of the earth's surface, he says he would rather not know the Nile's sources. He thinks some unexplored regions should remain as hunting grounds for the poetic imagination.”
“Well, there's something to be said for that, you know,” Mr. Brooke remarked, with an undeniably impartial mind.

“I fear it is merely another expression of his general imprecision and unwillingness to be thorough about anything. That would bode poorly in any profession, secular or sacred, even if he submitted to ordinary rules sufficiently to choose one.”

“Perhaps he has conscientious doubts about his own fitness,” Dorothea suggested, interested in finding a favourable explanation. “Law and medicine ought to be very serious professions to enter, shouldn't they? People's lives and fortunes depend on them.”

“Certainly. But I fear my young relation Will Ladislaw chiefly dislikes these professions because he dislikes steady application, and the learning that serves as a necessary tool without being charming or immediately appealing to a self-indulgent taste. I have emphasized to him Aristotle's admirably concise observation: to accomplish any work regarded as a goal, one must first exercise many lesser powers or acquired skills, and that requires patience. I have shown him my manuscript volumes, the product of years of labour in preparation for a work still unfinished. It has been useless. He answers careful reasoning of this sort by calling himself Pegasus, and every kind of assigned work ‘harness.’”
Celia laughed. It surprised her to discover that Mr. Casaubon could say something genuinely amusing.
“Well, you know, he might turn out another Byron, Chatterton or Churchill, something of that sort. There's no telling,” Mr. Brooke said. “Will you let him go to Italy, or wherever he wants?”
“Yes. I have agreed to give him a modest allowance for a year or so. He asks no more. I shall let freedom put him to the test.”

“That's very kind of you,” Dorothea said, looking up at him with delight. “It's noble. After all, people may have a calling within them that they don't yet clearly understand, mayn't they? Perhaps they seem idle and weak because they're still growing. I think we should be very patient with one another.”
“I suppose being engaged has taught you that patience is good,” Celia said as soon as they were alone, taking off their outdoor things.
“You mean I'm very impatient, Celia.”
“Yes, when people don't say and do exactly what you want.” Since the engagement, Celia had become less afraid of “saying things” to Dorothea. Cleverness seemed more pitiable to her than ever.
